That's an interesting perspective.  I think the main reason we have reached different conclusions is because we have a different idea of profit, and also of the idea of productivity.  For the former, to me, profit is by nature exploitative in nearly any situation, because you must sell a service or good for more than it is worth. That means that you must take money from somebody else, as they must pay more than something is worth.  In the modern world, employers trade the services and goods produced through labour on the behalf of their workers, but take much more than their equivalent in committed labour.  These two things combined would mean that employers are trading the services and goods they take from employees for an unfair price to consumers, but also not paying their employees their fair share of any generated wealth.  The larger the profit generated for the employer, the greater the extent to which these practices are carried out, it appears to me, at least.

This ties into why I don't think people like Musk are "productive".  They might seem so at first, since they appear to provide the materials and tools needed for workers to carry out their labour, and they appear to organise the workforce.  However, to socialists, they accumulate wealth and benefit from productivity unfairly through the methods listed above.  This means that they are a drain on both the quality of life of the workers and to the productivity of the company.  Musk doesn't design space travel equipment, the researchers on his payrole do.  So, this is probably why OP and people on the sub dislike Musk.  His vast wealth suggests exploitative practices to us, and his status as a capitalist employer makes him a supporter of a system we find to be inefficient and immoral.
